newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems meet Serb tormentors in Bosnia poll.
newsitem.headline: Moslems meet Serb tormentors in Bosnia poll.

text.p: Moslem voters came face-to-face with their Serb tormentors in the Bosnian village of Aliscici on Saturday for the first time in four years.
Some former neighbours greeted each other curtly, some chatted, and some said they never wanted to live together again.

The scene of the uneasy reunion was a polling station in a wrecked cafe when Moslem refugees "ethnically cleansed" from their homes in 1992 returned to the northwest Bosnian village to vote in nationwide elections.
In Aliscici, Serb homes perch on a lush green hillside unscathed by the Bosnian war. Little remains of the Moslem settlement at the foot of the hill but burnt-out shells.
Some of the Moslems, bussed into Serb-controlled territory from the nearby Moslem town of Sanski Most, shook with fear as they queued in a muddy yard under the gaze of Serb militia.

"I feel dreadful. Everywhere I turn I see nothing left," said 23-year-old Melita, who lost three brothers during the war when a Serb shell hit a sports hall where they were sheltering as refugees in the central Bosnian town of Travnik.

The NATO-led Peace Implementation Force IFOR staged a show of force to ensure peaceful voting in Aliscici, one of the tensest points in northwestern Bosnia. Armoured cars rumbled by the polling station and helicopters circled overhead.
Nothing could reassure Melita, who refused to give her family name. "IFOR may be standing by the road but it is not really secure," she said.
But for some of the Moslems, voting in the hostile environment -- voluntarily, as they could have cast their ballots back in Moslem-controlled Sanski Most -- offered a glimmer of hope for the future.
"This time we came here to vote," said 65-year-old Hamdija Jagic from the nearby Serb-controlled town of Prijedor. "Next time we will reach our homes and the third time we will live in our homes."
The response from some Serbs looking on was predictable.
"I don't understand why they have no shame and came back when they have opted for (Moslem) fundamentalism," said Zoran, a 26-year- old plain-clothes policeman.
"The only lasting solution is for us to stay apart, at least for some time to come," said Zoran, himself a refugee from the town of Bosanska Krupa a short distance away, in Moslem territory.

Despite all the horrors of the past four years, some villagers from the two communities chatted by the roadside just like any neighbours parted for several years. One Serb man patted a Moslem woman on the back and told her:
"Please say hello to your husband." REUTER
